title: How much? The amount of chemical change
summary: Balanced equations give mole ratios. Use them to find reacting masses, gas volumes and titration results, identify the limiting reactant, and calculate percentage yield and atom economy.

keyterms.definition: A chemical equation with equal numbers of each atom (and equal charge) on both sides; coefficients give mole ratios.
The ratio of amounts of substances in a reaction, taken from the coefficients of the balanced equation.
The reactant that is completely used up first and so determines the maximum amount of product.
A reactant present in more than the amount needed to react with the limiting reactant.
The maximum mass of product that could form from the limiting reactant, calculated from the equation.
(Molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of all reactants) × 100; a measure of efficiency and waste.
A technique in which one solution is added from a burette to a known volume of another until the reaction is just complete (end point).
Equivalence: reactants exactly in stoichiometric ratio. End point: when the indicator changes colour.
(s), (l), (g) and (aq) show the physical state of each species in an equation.

questions.prompt: What mass of CO₂ forms when 10.0 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.09 g mol⁻¹) decomposes completely? CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

questions.text: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 4.0 mol H₂ reacts with 3.0 mol O₂. The limiting reactant is ___.
questions.explanation: 4.0 mol H₂ needs only 2.0 mol O₂, so O₂ is in excess and H₂ runs out first.

questions.statement: The reactant with the smaller mass is always the limiting reactant.
questions.explanation: Compare moles divided by their coefficients, not masses.

questions.prompt: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. What volume of NH₃ forms from 30 dm³ of H₂ (excess N₂), at the same T and p?
questions.explanation: Gas volumes are in the mole ratio: 3 : 2, so 30 × 2/3 = 20 dm³.

questions.text: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 8.0 g and an actual yield of 6.0 g. The percentage yield is ___ %.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Theoretical yield is calculated from the limiting reactant.

questions.prompt: Why is the percentage yield usually below 100 %?
options: Side reactions, incomplete reaction and losses during purification
The limiting reactant is in excess
questions.explanation: Real processes lose product to side reactions, equilibria and transfers.

questions.text: The atom economy for making CaO from CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (M: CaO 56.08, CaCO₃ 100.09) is ___ %.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in calculating a reacting mass.
items: Calculate moles of the known substance
Use the mole ratio to find moles of the unknown
Convert moles to mass with M

questions.explanation: All reactant atoms end up in the single product, so there is no waste product.

questions.prompt: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH is neutralized by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl. What is [NaOH]?

questions.statement: At the equivalence point, reactants have been added in the stoichiometric ratio.
questions.explanation: The indicator end point should be chosen to match the equivalence point closely.

questions.text: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. 0.0050 mol H₂SO₄ reacts with ___ mol NaOH.

questions.prompt: Which piece of apparatus delivers an accurate fixed volume (e.g. 25.00 cm³) of solution into the flask?
questions.explanation: A volumetric pipette delivers one precise volume; the burette delivers variable volumes.

questions.prompt: Match each state symbol to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Use (l) for pure liquids such as water, (aq) for solutions.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an acid–base titration.
items: Rinse the burette with the titrant and fill it
Pipette a known volume of analyte into a conical flask
Add a few drops of indicator
Add titrant until the indicator just changes colour
questions.explanation: Concordant titres (within about 0.10 cm³) are averaged.
4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃: 4 Al and 6 O on each side.

questions.statement: Rinsing the conical flask with distilled water before a titration affects the result.
questions.explanation: Water does not change the moles of analyte delivered by the pipette, so the titre is unaffected.

questions.text: The ionic equation for any strong acid–strong base neutralization is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → ___.
questions.explanation: Spectator ions (e.g. Na⁺, Cl⁻) are left out of ionic equations.
